hdl-verification-001.question: What is a major difference between a description written in an HDL such as Verilog and a software program in a language such as C?
choices: An HDL description represents circuits that operate concurrently
An HDL description is a sequence of instructions executed one line at a time from the top
HDLs cannot use variables or conditional branches
hdl-verification-001.explanation: An HDL looks like a program, but logic synthesis turns what is written into gates and flip-flops. Every part of a circuit operates at all times, so multiple assign statements and always blocks work in parallel regardless of their order in the text. Thinking "do this, then that" as in software leads to unintended circuits, so it is important to picture the circuit being created while writing.
choiceNotes: Correct. Every part of the circuit is always operating at once.
That is the software way of thinking.
HDLs do use signals and conditional branches.

hdl-verification-002.question: What is the purpose of a module in Verilog?
choices: To define a circuit component with input and output ports so it can be used inside other modules
To pause program execution temporarily
To print simulation results on the screen
hdl-verification-002.explanation: A module defines a block of circuitry with input and output ports, representing anything from an adder or counter to an entire CPU. A defined module can be used as a component any number of times inside other modules (instantiation), with its ports wired together to build larger circuits. Circuits are built hierarchically, much like placing and wiring parts on a board.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the unit for building circuits hierarchically.
It does not pause execution.
Display uses $display and similar.

hdl-verification-003.question: What is the difference between wire and reg in Verilog?
choices: A reg always becomes a flip-flop and a wire always becomes combinational logic
wire represents connections driven by assign statements and the like; reg is a signal assigned inside always blocks, but a reg does not necessarily become a flip-flop
wire holds numbers and reg holds characters
hdl-verification-003.explanation: In Verilog, signals driven by assign statements or module outputs are declared wire, and signals assigned inside always blocks are declared reg. reg looks like short for register, but assigned inside always @(*) it becomes combinational logic, not a flip-flop. Whether a flip-flop results depends on whether the value is updated on a clock edge. SystemVerilog allows both to be written as logic.
choiceNotes: Despite the name, a reg can become combinational logic.
Correct. A reg in always @(*) becomes combinational logic.
Neither is a character type.

hdl-verification-004.question: What circuit does the Verilog assign statement above represent?
choices: Combinational logic ORing c with the AND of a and b; y changes immediately when inputs change
A flip-flop that updates y on every clock
A circuit that computes once and never changes afterward
hdl-verification-004.explanation: An assign statement, called a continuous assignment, represents wiring in which the value of the right-hand expression is always reflected on the left-hand signal. If any input on the right changes, the output y changes right away (after gate delay). This example becomes combinational logic made of an AND gate and an OR gate. It has no memory, so holding a value requires an always block updated by a clock.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is called a continuous assignment.
No clock is involved.
The output follows every input change.

hdl-verification-005.question: What circuit does logic synthesis create from the Verilog above?
choices: An AND gate of d and clk
A D flip-flop that captures d on the rising clock edge
A latch that passes d whenever clk is 1
hdl-verification-005.explanation: "always @(posedge clk)" means the assignments inside happen only at the instant of the rising clock edge, and synthesis turns this into an edge-triggered flip-flop. q holds the value d had at the rising edge until the next one. Almost all storage in synchronous circuits is written this way. It must be distinguished from a latch, which responds to clock level rather than edges.
choiceNotes: The clock serves as an edge trigger; no AND is built.
Correct. posedge means the rising edge.
It is edge-triggered, so it is not a latch.

hdl-verification-006.question: How does Verilog's nonblocking assignment (<=) behave?
choices: The left side updates immediately, and the next line sees the new value
All right-hand sides at that time step are evaluated first, and then the left-hand sides are updated together
The result is discarded and nothing changes
hdl-verification-006.explanation: With nonblocking assignment, at the clock edge every <= right-hand side is first evaluated using the old values, and only then are all left-hand sides updated together. This mirrors real hardware, where many flip-flops on the same clock capture their pre-edge inputs simultaneously. That is why nonblocking assignment is the rule for describing clocked sequential logic.
choiceNotes: That is the behavior of blocking assignment (=).
Correct. It matches flip-flops capturing values simultaneously.
The value is updated.

hdl-verification-007.question: In the code above, a = 0 and b = 1 just before a rising clock edge. What are a and b after the edge?
choices: a = 1, b = 0 (they swap)
hdl-verification-007.explanation: With nonblocking assignment, both right sides (b's old value 1 and a's old value 0) are evaluated first, then a gets 1 and b gets 0 simultaneously, so they swap. As a circuit, the two flip-flops' outputs are wired to each other's inputs. With blocking assignment (=), line 1 sets a to 1, and line 2 gives b the new a, 1, so both end up as 1.
choiceNotes: Correct. Both right sides use the old values.
That is the result with "=".
No value is lost.

hdl-verification-008.question: Intending a two-stage shift register, someone wrote the code above with blocking assignments (=). What goes wrong?
choices: q2 receives q1 updated at the same edge (that is, d), so the circuit delays by only one stage
q1 and q2 stay 0 forever
It correctly becomes a two-stage shift register with no problem
hdl-verification-008.explanation: With blocking assignment, line 1 immediately updates q1 to d, and line 2 gives q2 the updated q1, which is d. So q2 equals q1, and both simulation and the synthesized circuit delay by only one stage. Writing "q1 <= d; q2 <= q1;" gives q2 the pre-edge q1, yielding the intended two-stage shift register. Reversing the lines might also work, but that invites mistakes.
choiceNotes: Correct. Writing it with <= gives two stages.
The values do update.
With blocking assignment, the next line uses the new value.

hdl-verification-009.question: What is the common guideline for choosing assignment types in Verilog?
choices: Use only blocking assignment (=) everywhere
Use nonblocking (<=) for clocked sequential logic and blocking (=) in combinational always blocks
Mix both arbitrarily in the same always block
hdl-verification-009.explanation: Writing sequential logic with nonblocking assignments matches hardware where all flip-flops capture values simultaneously, so results do not depend on statement order or on the execution order of other always blocks. Combinational logic naturally computes intermediate values from top to bottom, so blocking assignments are used there. It is also important not to mix the two within one always block.
choiceNotes: Blocking in sequential logic often yields unintended circuits.
Correct. It keeps simulation and hardware behavior consistent.
Mixing makes behavior hard to follow and error-prone.

hdl-verification-010.question: What does writing "always @(*)" mean in Verilog?
choices: It describes a flip-flop that runs on every rising clock edge
It runs only once at the start of simulation
It runs whenever any signal read inside the block changes, describing combinational logic
hdl-verification-010.explanation: The list inside @( ) after always is called the sensitivity list and specifies which signal changes trigger the block. Writing "*" automatically includes every signal read in the block, correctly describing combinational logic. Listing signals by hand invites omissions, so "@(*)" or SystemVerilog's always_comb is the safe choice for combinational logic.
choiceNotes: Clock edges are specified with posedge and similar.
Running once is what initial does.
Correct. It is like listing every signal read automatically.

hdl-verification-011.question: Intending combinational logic, someone wrote the code above. What problem can occur?
choices: b is removed from the circuit and y becomes equal to a
Synthesis fails and no circuit is produced
When only b changes, simulation does not update y, so it disagrees with the synthesized circuit, where y follows b
hdl-verification-011.explanation: A simulator runs the block only when a signal in the sensitivity list changes, so when only b changes, y keeps its stale value. Logic synthesis, however, ignores the list and builds an AND gate from the block's contents, so in the real circuit changes in b do reach y. This is dangerous: simulation looks right while the hardware behaves differently. Writing "@(*)" prevents it.
choiceNotes: Synthesis builds an AND gate.
Most synthesis tools warn but still build the circuit.
Correct. It is the classic sensitivity-list omission.

hdl-verification-012.question: Intending combinational logic, someone writes the code above. What does logic synthesis produce?
choices: Combinational logic where y automatically becomes 0 when en is 0
A clocked D flip-flop
Because y must hold its value when en is 0, an unintended latch is created
hdl-verification-012.explanation: When en is 0 nothing is assigned to y, so y must remember its previous value. Combinational logic has no memory, so synthesis creates a latch to hold it. Latches complicate timing analysis and can malfunction from glitches, so unintended ones are avoided. Assigning a value in every case, for example "else y = 0;", yields combinational logic.
choiceNotes: Nothing assigns 0, so it does not become 0.
No clock is used, so it is not a flip-flop.
Correct. The missing else is the cause.

hdl-verification-013.question: Why does the code above create a latch, and what is the fix?
choices: Three inputs are used in the case; reduce them to two
No value is assigned to y when sel = 2'b11; add a default clause so every case assigns a value
always @(*) is used; change it to always @(posedge clk)
hdl-verification-013.explanation: sel is 2 bits with four possible values, but 2'b11 is not handled, so y must keep its previous value in that case, creating a latch. Specifying a value for every remaining case, such as "default: y = 0;", or assigning y a default value before the case statement yields combinational logic. Latches from incomplete conditions are a common mistake for HDL beginners.
choiceNotes: The number of inputs is not the cause.
Correct. Every case must be covered.
That would create flip-flops, a different circuit.

hdl-verification-014.question: Which coding style is commonly used to prevent unintended latches in combinational always blocks?
choices: Write as many branches as possible and omit else
Assign default values to every output signal at the top of the block before the conditional logic
Declare all outputs as wire and assign them inside always
hdl-verification-014.explanation: Putting defaults such as "y = 0; valid = 0;" at the top ensures every output is assigned at least its default on whatever path the later branches take, so nothing needs to hold its value and no latch forms. This is especially helpful for state machine outputs with many conditions. With SystemVerilog's always_comb, tools also warn if a latch is inferred.
choiceNotes: Omitting else causes latches.
Correct. Every path then assigns a value.
A wire cannot be assigned in an always block.

hdl-verification-015.question: Which Verilog construct is ignored by logic synthesis and does not become hardware (a simulation-only construct)?
choices: An assign statement
always @(posedge clk)
A delay specification such as #10
hdl-verification-015.explanation: "#10" advances simulation time by 10 units, but logic synthesis cannot build delays, so it ignores them. Real circuit delays are set by the gates and wiring used. Testbench constructs such as $display and file I/O likewise do not become hardware. Mixing such constructs into synthesizable RTL causes simulation and hardware behavior to diverge.
choiceNotes: An assign statement becomes combinational logic.
This becomes flip-flops.
Correct. Delays are determined by the placed-and-routed circuit.

hdl-verification-016.question: When the code above, which counts the 1s in 8-bit d, is synthesized, what kind of circuit results?
choices: A sequential circuit counting one bit per clock over 8 cycles
The loop is unrolled into eight steps, giving combinational logic with a chain of adders
For loops cannot be synthesized, so it errors out
hdl-verification-016.explanation: An HDL for loop does not reuse the same circuit repeatedly as software would; synthesis unrolls it into as many copies as there are iterations. Here it becomes combinational logic with eight adders in a row, computing everything within one clock. Many iterations make the circuit large and slow, so care is needed. To compute over time with less hardware, write a clocked state machine instead.
choiceNotes: No clock is used, so it does not count over time.
Correct. The fixed iteration count allows unrolling.
For loops with fixed bounds are synthesizable.

hdl-verification-017.question: What type of reset does the code above have, and how does it behave?
choices: A synchronous reset: q becomes 0 only at a rising clock edge while rst_n is 0
An asynchronous reset: when rst_n goes to 0, q becomes 0 immediately without waiting for a clock
q becomes 0 when rst_n goes to 1
hdl-verification-017.explanation: Because "negedge rst_n" is in the sensitivity list, the block also runs the instant rst_n falls from 1 to 0, and q becomes 0 regardless of the clock. This is an asynchronous reset. The "_n" suffix is a convention for active-low signals. It can reset even when the clock is stopped, but the timing of reset release needs care.
choiceNotes: The reset edge is also a trigger, so it is not synchronous.
Correct. The reset edge is in the sensitivity list.
_n indicates active-low.

hdl-verification-018.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous resets?
choices: A synchronous reset acts regardless of the clock; an asynchronous one only at clock edges
A synchronous reset takes effect only at clock edges; an asynchronous reset takes effect immediately regardless of the clock
They behave identically; only the names differ
hdl-verification-018.explanation: A synchronous reset samples the reset signal at clock edges like any other input, which eases timing analysis, but it cannot reset without a running clock. An asynchronous reset uses the flip-flop's reset pin directly, so it acts at once even without a clock, but if release happens near a clock edge, flip-flops may come out of reset at different cycles.
choiceNotes: It is the other way around.
Correct. Each has advantages and caveats.
They differ in when the reset takes effect.

hdl-verification-019.question: In circuits using asynchronous reset, why is reset release (the 0-to-1 transition) synchronized to the clock through two flip-flops before distribution?
choices: To delay asserting reset by two clocks for safety
To make the reset signal twice as fast
If release lands near a clock edge, flip-flops may leave reset on different cycles or become unstable, so release is aligned to the clock
hdl-verification-019.explanation: If an asynchronous reset is released just before or after a clock edge, the timing requirements for release are violated, and one flip-flop may start in this cycle while another starts in the next. This can start a state machine in an illegal state. A reset synchronizer applies reset immediately but aligns only its release to the clock through two flip-flops before distributing it.
choiceNotes: Assertion still takes effect immediately.
It does not change speed.
Correct. Assertion is asynchronous; release is synchronous.

hdl-verification-020.question: What is the basic structure of a state machine written in an HDL?
choices: Only memory to remember the state, with no logic
Only output logic, with no memory of state
A register holding the current state, combinational logic choosing the next state, and combinational logic producing outputs
hdl-verification-020.explanation: A state machine keeps the current state in a flip-flop register, determines the next state from the current state and inputs with combinational logic, and updates the state at the clock edge. Outputs are produced from the current state (and inputs) by combinational logic. Many circuits that follow a procedure, such as protocol controllers, vending machines and traffic lights, are written as state machines.
choiceNotes: Logic to determine the next state is needed.
A state register is required.
Correct. The state is updated by the clock.

hdl-verification-021.question: In the state machine above, why does the second always block begin with "next = state;"?
choices: To stay in the current state when no condition matches and to assign next in every case, preventing a latch
To return the state to IDLE every time
To stop the clock
hdl-verification-021.explanation: Splitting a state machine into a register block that updates the state and a combinational block that computes the next state is a common style. In the combinational block, if nothing assigns next when start or done is 0, a latch forms. Starting with "next = state;" clearly expresses staying in the current state when no condition matches, while preventing the latch.
choiceNotes: Correct. It sets the default value first.
It holds the current state rather than resetting to IDLE.
It has nothing to do with the clock.

hdl-verification-022.question: What characterizes a Mealy state machine?
choices: Outputs depend only on the state and do not change until the next clock
Outputs depend on both current state and inputs, so input changes appear at the output within the same cycle
It is combinational logic with no state
hdl-verification-022.explanation: In a Mealy machine the output logic looks at inputs as well as the current state, so outputs change with inputs without waiting for a clock, reacting one cycle sooner. It may also need fewer states. But a combinational path runs from inputs to outputs, so input glitches can appear at outputs and timing paths get longer. Outputs are sometimes re-registered through flip-flops.
choiceNotes: That describes a Moore machine.
Correct. It reacts faster but passes input glitches to outputs more easily.
It is sequential logic with state.

hdl-verification-023.question: What is a characteristic of one-hot encoding for state machine states?
choices: It encodes states in binary to minimize flip-flops
All flip-flops are always 1
It uses one flip-flop per state with exactly one set at a time, so next-state and output logic tend to be simple and fast
hdl-verification-023.explanation: One-hot encoding represents, say, four states as 0001, 0010, 0100 and 1000, assigning one flip-flop to each state. It needs more flip-flops, but checking whether the machine is in a state means looking at a single bit, so next-state and output logic is shallow and fast. It is common on flip-flop-rich FPGAs, while binary encoding is used when flip-flop count must be minimized.
choiceNotes: That is binary encoding.
Exactly one is 1 at any time.
Correct. It is popular on flip-flop-rich FPGAs.

hdl-verification-024.question: For a state machine with three states, how many flip-flops are needed to store the state (binary encoding / one-hot encoding)?
hdl-verification-024.explanation: Binary encoding numbers the states in binary, so three states fit in 2 bits (two flip-flops): 00, 01 and 10. One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, so three. Binary leaves the unused code 11, so it is safer to define its destination with a default branch, letting the machine recover if noise ever puts it there.
choiceNotes: It is the other way around.
Correct. Two bits can represent up to four states.
One bit can represent only two states.

hdl-verification-025.question: In the 4-bit counter above, when count is 15 and a rising clock edge arrives, what does count become?
choices: It stays at 15
hdl-verification-025.explanation: A 4-bit reg can represent only 0 to 15. Adding 1 to 15 (1111 in binary) gives 10000, but the top bit does not fit and is dropped, so count returns to 0000, that is, 0. This property is used to build counters that repeat every fixed number of steps. Unintended overflow, however, causes bugs, so signal bit widths always deserve attention.
choiceNotes: The 4-bit range is 0 to 15.
Correct. Four bits cannot hold 16, so it wraps to 0.
The addition happens and wraps to 0.

hdl-verification-026.question: In Verilog, two 8-bit signals a and b are added and assigned to an 8-bit signal s (assign s = a + b;). What should be watched for?
choices: Adding two 8-bit values cannot be written in Verilog
The result is automatically widened to 16 bits
If the sum exceeds 255, the ninth-bit carry is discarded, so make s 9 bits if the carry is needed
hdl-verification-026.explanation: The sum of two 8-bit values can reach 255 + 255 = 510, which needs 9 bits. If s is 8 bits, the carry is silently dropped, and 200 + 100 becomes 44, for example. To keep the carry, declare s as 9 bits. Verilog does not reject assignments between different widths but truncates or extends them, so checking width mismatches with a lint tool is effective.
choiceNotes: It can be written normally.
An 8-bit destination truncates it to 8 bits.
Correct. The result is truncated to the destination width.

hdl-verification-027.question: Intending a to be signed -1, someone wrote the code above, and gt became 1. Why?
choices: Without a signed declaration, a was compared as unsigned 255
Comparisons in Verilog always return 1
8'hFF equals 0
hdl-verification-027.explanation: Verilog treats signals as unsigned unless declared signed, so 8'hFF is 255, and 255 > 1 is true. Declaring a as "wire signed [7:0]" and also making the constant signed, as in 8'sd1, compares a as two's-complement -1, giving 0. Sized or based constants such as 8'd1 are unsigned, and if any operand in an expression is unsigned the whole expression is evaluated unsigned, so declaring only a as signed still leaves gt at 1. Signed arithmetic therefore requires keeping all operand types consistent.
choiceNotes: Correct. Signed treatment requires a signed declaration.
Comparisons yield 0 or 1 depending on the values.
8'hFF is 255 (or -1 if signed).

hdl-verification-028.question: Which set of values makes up the four-state logic used in Verilog simulation?
choices: 0, 1, X (unknown) and Z (high impedance)
True, false, up and down
hdl-verification-028.explanation: Besides 0 and 1, Verilog signals can be X (unknown) and Z (high impedance, undriven). Uninitialized registers and signals with conflicting drivers become X, while unconnected wires and tri-state lines whose drivers are disabled become Z. Spotting X or Z in simulation is a major clue to finding bugs.
choiceNotes: Correct. These represent real circuit conditions.
They are not the numbers 0 to 3.
Those are not logic values.

hdl-verification-029.question: In simulation, a register without reset starts as X. What happens in the real chip?
choices: At power-on it becomes either 0 or 1, but which one is not determined
It stays stuck at a voltage midway between 0 and 1
It is always 0 in the real chip
hdl-verification-029.explanation: A real flip-flop settles to a stable 0 or 1 at power-on, but which one varies with the chip, location, temperature and so on and is not determined. The X in simulation represents "unknown which". If that value affects circuit behavior, it must be set by reset. Registers in data paths that are always written before use sometimes omit reset.
choiceNotes: Correct. That is why reset or initialization matters.
A flip-flop settles to either 0 or 1.
It is not guaranteed to be 0.

hdl-verification-030.question: In the code above, when sel is X, Verilog simulation selects b for y. Why is this a problem for verification?
choices: y always becomes X and simulation stops
The real chip also always selects b when sel is X
X is treated as false and a definite value b appears, so the bug of an unknown sel is hidden in simulation
hdl-verification-030.explanation: A Verilog if statement treats an X condition as false and executes the else branch. So y gets the definite value b, and the bug of an unknown sel is hidden in simulation. In the real circuit sel is either 0 or 1, and a may be selected. This is called X-optimism and is countered by coding styles that propagate X or by adding assertions that detect X.
choiceNotes: y does not become X; it becomes b.
In the real chip either a or b could be selected.
Correct. This is known as X-optimism.

hdl-verification-031.question: Which statement about tri-state descriptions that output Z (high impedance) in an HDL is generally correct?
choices: All internal signals are normally built with tri-states
They are used for bidirectional pins connecting off-chip, while internal signals normally use multiplexers
Z means the same as 0, so it can be used anywhere
hdl-verification-031.explanation: A tri-state lets several circuits share one wire by disconnecting their outputs, and is used for bidirectional pins such as external bus or memory data lines. Inside a chip it risks two drivers colliding or no one driving the line so it floats, and it complicates timing analysis. So internal signals are normally selected with multiplexers instead.
choiceNotes: Multiplexers are the norm internally.
Correct. Internal tri-states complicate timing and verification.
Z means undriven, which is different from 0.

hdl-verification-032.question: Which describes a testbench used in HDL verification?
choices: Factory equipment for manufacturing circuits
A simulation-only description that drives inputs to the circuit under test and checks whether outputs are correct; it is not synthesized
An instrument for measuring circuit power
hdl-verification-032.explanation: A testbench is HDL code that instantiates the design under test (DUT), generates clocks, resets and input signals, and observes outputs. Because it is never synthesized, it can freely use simulation-only features such as delays, file I/O and display statements. It sometimes takes as much effort as the design itself, or more.
choiceNotes: It is not factory equipment.
Correct. It is a test environment wrapped around the design.
It is a simulation description, not a physical instrument.

hdl-verification-033.question: What is the period of the clock generated by the testbench code above (time unit 1 ns)?
choices: 5 ns
20 ns
10 ns
hdl-verification-033.explanation: "always #5 clk = ~clk;" keeps toggling clk every 5 time units. Two toggles, 0 to 1 and 1 to 0, make one period, so the period is 10 ns and the frequency 100 MHz. This is how testbenches generate clocks. Real circuit clocks come from oscillators or PLLs, so this code never becomes hardware.
choiceNotes: 5 ns is half a period.
That counts four toggle intervals.
Correct. It toggles every 5 ns, so one period is 10 ns.

hdl-verification-034.question: In a testbench, changing a design input with a blocking assignment at the same instant as the rising clock edge can cause problems. Which pairs the reason with a fix correctly?
choices: Whether the design captures the old or new value depends on execution order (a race); change inputs away from the clock edge or with nonblocking assignments
The clock frequency automatically drops; make the clock faster
Blocking assignments are not allowed in testbenches; use assign everywhere
hdl-verification-034.explanation: When the testbench updates an input at the same instant the design's flip-flops sample it, the captured value can be old or new depending on which the simulator executes first. This is a simulation race, and results may even differ between simulators. It is prevented by changing inputs on the falling edge or slightly after the edge, or by using nonblocking assignments or SystemVerilog clocking blocks.
choiceNotes: Correct. It avoids a simulation race.
The frequency does not change.
Blocking assignments are allowed in testbenches.

hdl-verification-035.question: What characterizes a self-checking testbench?
choices: A person visually inspects waveforms and judges correctness every time
It automatically compares outputs with expected values and reports pass or fail itself
The circuit is manufactured and then checked in silicon
hdl-verification-035.explanation: Checking waveforms by eye is handy for small circuits, but as tests multiply, mistakes slip through and rechecking after every change is impractical. A self-checking testbench computes or looks up the expected output for each input, compares it automatically with the design's output and reports any mismatch as an error. Thousands of tests can run unattended overnight with only the results to review.
choiceNotes: That is not self-checking.
Correct. Large numbers of tests can run automatically.
It runs in simulation before manufacturing.

hdl-verification-036.question: What is the purpose of a reference (golden) model written in C or similar in verification?
choices: To hand it to the factory as the manufacturing blueprint
To compute the same function another way and use its results as expected values to compare with the design's outputs
To slow the circuit down so it is easier to watch
hdl-verification-036.explanation: A reference model is a straightforward software implementation of the function the circuit must perform, without regard to timing. Feeding the same inputs to both the circuit and the model and comparing results generates expected values automatically, even for large volumes of random input. If built by the same person with the same misunderstanding as the design, it will miss bugs, so it should be written independently from the specification.
choiceNotes: Layout data, not a C model, goes to the factory.
Correct. Agreement with an independently built model is checked.
It does not change speed.

hdl-verification-037.question: What is the main purpose of dumping simulation results to a file in a format such as VCD?
choices: To view signal changes over time in a waveform viewer and investigate bugs
To send the circuit design to the factory
To speed up the simulation
hdl-verification-037.explanation: VCD (Value Change Dump) is a standard file format recording when and how each signal changed during simulation. Opening it in a waveform viewer shows signal changes clock by clock along a time axis, so you can trace where a value first deviated from expectation. Recording every signal produces huge files, so the dump is sometimes limited to the time range or signals of interest.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a basic debugging tool.
It is not data sent to the factory.
Dumping actually slows simulation.

hdl-verification-038.question: Why should the random seed be recorded in tests that use random inputs?
choices: The same seed reproduces the same input sequence, so a bug that was found can be re-examined any number of times
Recording the seed generates random numbers faster
Simulation will not start unless the seed is recorded
hdl-verification-038.explanation: Simulation random numbers are pseudo-random, generated by a fixed procedure from a seed, so the same seed gives the same sequence. If a random test finds a bug but the seed is unknown, the situation cannot be recreated to investigate the cause or to confirm a fix. The standard practice is to run many tests with different seeds and record the seed of any failure.
choiceNotes: Correct. Bugs that cannot be reproduced are hard to fix.
It has nothing to do with speed.
Simulation starts without it.

hdl-verification-039.question: Which describes constrained random verification in SystemVerilog?
choices: Input values are generated randomly within constraints allowed by the specification, broadly exercising cases people might not think of
Input values are generated completely at random, including many values outside the specification
People write every input value by hand
hdl-verification-039.explanation: Tests people devise (directed tests) tend to miss bugs in combinations the designer did not anticipate. Constrained random verification states constraints such as "addresses are multiples of 4" or "length is 1 to 256" and generates random inputs within them, exercising many cases with only meaningful inputs. Coverage measures which cases were hit, and gaps are filled by adjusting constraints or adding directed tests.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is combined with coverage measurement.
Mostly out-of-spec inputs make for meaningless verification.
That is directed testing.

hdl-verification-040.question: Which describes regression testing in circuit design?
choices: Testing only the newly added feature once
Studying how circuit performance declines year by year
Re-running the existing tests after every design change to confirm that previously working features have not broken
hdl-verification-040.explanation: Fixing a bug or adding a feature can break something elsewhere unexpectedly. Regression testing automatically re-runs every test built so far to check that previously passing tests still pass. Large designs run thousands of tests almost daily and track the results in a summary. This automation is possible only with self-checking testbenches.
choiceNotes: Changes can affect other parts too.
It is unrelated to statistical regression analysis.
Correct. It checks that fixes have not caused new bugs.

hdl-verification-041.question: What is an advantage of SystemVerilog's logic type?
choices: It can be assigned from either assign or always without worrying about the wire/reg distinction (for single-driver signals)
It is guaranteed to become a flip-flop
It cannot hold X or Z, so simulation runs faster
hdl-verification-041.explanation: In Verilog, signals assigned in always blocks had to be reg and those driven by assign had to be wire, so changing usage meant editing declarations and invited errors. SystemVerilog's logic can be assigned either way, so it covers most cases on its own. Signals with multiple drivers, such as tri-state buses, still use wire. logic is a four-state type including X and Z.
choiceNotes: Correct. Declaration mistakes decrease.
Whether a flip-flop results depends on the coding.
logic is four-state; the two-state type is bit.

hdl-verification-042.question: What is the advantage of using SystemVerilog's always_ff and always_comb instead of Verilog's always?
choices: always_ff always doubles circuit speed
always_comb makes simulation unnecessary
Tools know the designer's intent (flip-flops or combinational logic) and can warn when the result differs, for example a latch
hdl-verification-042.explanation: Verilog's always can describe flip-flops, combinational logic or latches, so tools do not know the designer's intent. Writing always_ff declares flip-flops and always_comb declares combinational logic, so tools can issue warnings or errors when, for example, an incomplete condition infers a latch. always_comb also derives its sensitivity automatically from the signals it reads.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with speed.
Simulation is still needed.
Correct. always_comb also determines its sensitivity list automatically.

hdl-verification-043.question: What is the advantage of writing a module with a parameter as above?
choices: Using a parameter automatically makes the circuit faster
The parameter value can be changed freely while the chip is running
Specifying W at each use creates adders of different widths, such as 8 or 16 bits, from the same code
hdl-verification-043.explanation: A parameter is a constant whose value can be specified when the module is used. Making bit widths or FIFO depths parameters lets one description be reused at various sizes, reducing the effort and errors of writing similar circuits repeatedly. Values are fixed at synthesis, and a circuit of the matching size is built for each. They do not change while the chip runs, so settings that must change at run time are held in registers.
choiceNotes: Speed does not change.
It is a constant fixed at synthesis and cannot change at run time.
Correct. It makes design reuse easier.

hdl-verification-044.question: What does the generate statement above do?
choices: It reuses one fifo four times over four clocks
It displays the fifo four times only during simulation
It creates four instances of the fifo module, each connected to a different element of din and dout
hdl-verification-044.explanation: A for loop inside a generate block expands its contents for each genvar value, replicating hardware descriptions. Here four fifo instances, g[0].u_fifo through g[3].u_fifo, are created, each connected to din[i] and dout[i]. Making the channel or bit count a parameter lets the number of instances change accordingly, so regularly structured circuits can be written concisely.
choiceNotes: It does not reuse; four circuits are placed side by side.
It creates hardware, not display output.
Correct. It is expanded into four circuits at synthesis.

hdl-verification-045.question: What is the role of a lint tool in HDL verification?
choices: A device that removes lint from chips
A tool for displaying simulation waveforms attractively
Examining code without simulation to find problems such as width mismatches, unintended latches and unsynthesizable constructs
hdl-verification-045.explanation: A lint tool statically checks HDL code against rules and flags constructs that are legal but prone to problems, such as assignments between different widths, incomplete sensitivity lists, inferred latches, mixed blocking and nonblocking assignments and clocking mistakes. It runs without any tests, so using it from early in design reduces later verification effort.
choiceNotes: It is not a physical cleaning device.
It is not a waveform viewer.
Correct. It finds mistakes early and cheaply.

hdl-verification-046.question: What is the main purpose of simulating the post-synthesis or post-layout gate-level netlist with delay information?
choices: To run many tests faster than RTL simulation
To check issues invisible in RTL simulation, such as initialization or reset bugs, synthesis differences and delay-related problems
To reduce circuit area
hdl-verification-046.explanation: RTL simulation is fast but cannot reveal unknown-value problems hidden by X-optimism, or cases where synthesis produced a circuit different from the description. Gate-level simulation exercises the actual gates and flip-flops, and with each gate's and wire's delay supplied in SDF format, delay-related problems also show up. It is very slow, so it is generally run on a limited set of tests.
choiceNotes: Gate-level simulation is far slower.
Correct. Delay information is supplied in formats such as SDF.
It does not change area.

hdl-verification-047.question: What is a structure like the code above, where a combinational output feeds back to its own input without passing through a flip-flop, called, and why should it be avoided?
choices: It is a combinational loop; it can oscillate or never settle, and timing analysis becomes impossible
It is a pipeline, and the circuit becomes too fast
It is a shift register, and data is lost
hdl-verification-047.explanation: With a determining b and b determining a and no flip-flop in between, values can circulate with every gate delay and oscillate, or settle to whatever the delay differences dictate. Latch-like memory can also form unintentionally. Static timing analysis cannot handle paths that form a loop. When feedback is needed, a flip-flop must be inserted so the value updates once per clock.
choiceNotes: Correct. Many tools issue errors or warnings.
A pipeline is divided by flip-flops.
A shift register is built from flip-flops.

hdl-verification-048.question: When the code above is synthesized for an FPGA, how is it generally implemented?
choices: It cannot be synthesized and causes an error
It becomes 256 independent adders
It is inferred as an 8-bit × 256-word memory and mapped to the FPGA's built-in block RAM
hdl-verification-048.explanation: When a reg array is written and read synchronously with the clock in a standard pattern, synthesis tools recognize (infer) it as memory and map it to FPGA block RAM or ASIC memory macros. Making the read synchronous too is the key to matching block RAM; an asynchronous read may instead be built from many flip-flops or a different kind of memory.
choiceNotes: A reg array can be synthesized as memory.
No addition is involved.
Correct. Written in a standard pattern, it is recognized as memory.

hdl-verification-049.question: In combinational logic, how does a long if/else-if chain compare with a case statement whose conditions are mutually exclusive?
choices: An if/else-if chain implies priority on earlier conditions and tends to be deep and slow, while a case tends to become parallel selection
Both styles always synthesize to exactly the same circuit
case cannot be synthesized; only if can
hdl-verification-049.explanation: An if/else-if chain means "if the first condition holds take it, otherwise check the next", implying a priority circuit like a priority encoder, with one multiplexer per condition in series and long delay. A case selecting on mutually exclusive values tends to become a parallel structure like a single large multiplexer and is faster. Modern synthesis tools, however, often optimize either form.
choiceNotes: Correct. The difference is whether conditions have priority.
Circuits can differ depending on priority.
case is synthesizable too.

hdl-verification-050.question: What is the difference between Verilog's equality operators "==" and "==="?
choices: == yields X if X or Z is involved, while === compares X and Z literally as values and always yields 0 or 1
== and === behave identically
=== compares three values at once
hdl-verification-050.explanation: == behaves like a hardware comparator, so if either operand contains an X or Z bit, the result is X (unknown). === is called case equality and compares X as X and Z as Z literally, so a testbench can use it to check whether an output has become X. Real circuits cannot distinguish X or Z, so === is not synthesizable and is a testbench-only operator.
choiceNotes: Correct. === is used mainly in testbenches.
They treat X and Z differently.
It compares two values.
